Messages.Author: Jeff Haar
Messages.Body:
Does this change the legality of the mutual withdrawl? It seems that
at this point the judges responsibility is to determine if there is
enough time to facilitate additional ousts, since with infinite time
there certainly is a reasonable chance to merit additonal play.

I guess my fundamental question is:
1) What precisely are the rules for tournaments, outside of mechanical
considerations? What does the 'play the win' concept really mean in a
tournament setting?

There are so many gray and confusing situations that the concept seems
somewhat inadequate, at least to me. I could find no dirth of
questions the 'play to win' concept does not put into crystalline
focus.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Jeff Haar wrote:
> Does this change the legality of the mutual withdrawl? It seems that

What "this"?

> at this point the judges responsibility is to determine if there is
> enough time to facilitate additional ousts, since with infinite time
> there certainly is a reasonable chance to merit additonal play.
>
> I guess my fundamental question is:
> 1) What precisely are the rules for tournaments, outside of mechanical
> considerations? What does the 'play the win' concept really mean in a
> tournament setting?

That each player must play to win (based on the information available to
him or her at the time) and, if unable to win, must play to maximize
his or her VP accumulation.

> There are so many gray and confusing situations that the concept seems
> somewhat inadequate, at least to me. I could find no dirth of
> questions the 'play to win' concept does not put into crystalline
> focus.

Gray areas are what judges are for.
If everything were in crystalline focus, we wouldn't need judges.

If your idea of a concept in crystalline focus is such that the
meaning is different between players, then it matches my idea of
a gray area (quite far from my idea of a concept being in crystalline
focus).

> pretty sure in a tournament I can do anything I would like and if the
> judge bothered to care I could explain it within the 'play to win'
> framework. Not that I actually expect any judge to be that hands on.

If the set of things you "would like" is limited to things that
can be explained away under the "play to win" rule, sure. There
are trivial examples of things that one can do that violate
such the rule, regardless of explanations and conjecture, though.
